title: The boy in the temple (Luke 2:41–52)
hook: twelve-year-old Jesus goes missing for three days and is found asking questions
tomorrow: The wild man by the river

segments.voice: Yesterday, the flight into Egypt, a family running by night. Your line was he was a refugee first. Did you stop to picture one family? Day forty-six.

Every parent knows the feeling. You turn around in a crowded store and your kid isn't there. Your stomach drops. Now stretch that feeling out to three days. Mary and Joseph go up to Jerusalem every year for Passover, Luke says, and this year Jesus is twelve. When the feast ends they start home, traveling with a big group of relatives and neighbors, and they assume he's somewhere in the crowd. A whole day's walk later they look for him, and he's gone. They turn around. Three days of searching a packed city. Today, the boy in the temple.
screen: `WHERE'S THE KID?` → `A WHOLE DAY'S WALK.` → `THREE DAYS OF SEARCHING.`

segments.voice: They find him in the temple courts, and look at what he's doing. In the King James Bible: "sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions." Doctors here means teachers, the rabbis and scholars of the law. He isn't lecturing them. He's listening, and asking. Luke says everyone who heard him was astonished at his understanding and his answers. Then Mary speaks, and every parent will recognize it: "Son, why hast thou thus dealt with us? behold, thy father and I have sought thee sorrowing." And the boy's answer is the first thing Jesus ever says in Luke's Gospel: "How is it that ye sought me? wist ye not that I must be about my Father's business?" Here's a small puzzle. The Greek is short and can be read two ways: about my Father's business, or in my Father's house. Translators still choose between them. Either way, the first words he speaks point to God as his Father. And his parents, Luke says plainly, didn't understand. He goes home with them and is obedient to them, and Mary, again, keeps all these sayings in her heart. This is the only story in the four Gospels from the years between his infancy and his adult life. Eighteen years or so of silence, and the one scene we're given is a boy asking questions in the house of God. Then one line for everything after: "And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and man." He grew. Even he grew, a little at a time.
screen: `FOUND AMONG THE TEACHERS.` · `HEARING THEM, AND ASKING THEM.` · `MY FATHER'S BUSINESS, OR HOUSE?` · `THE ONLY STORY FROM THOSE YEARS.` · then, large: `JESUS INCREASED IN WISDOM AND STATURE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let yourself get quiet. Now look for a question you've been carrying. About God, about your life, about something you were taught that never quite made sense. A real one, not a polite one. Some people hide their questions because they think faith means having answers. The boy in this story sits in the temple asking. So find yours. Say it to yourself plainly, in one sentence. If you pray, you can bring it to God just as it is. The bell holds the time.
The boy in the temple. Twelve years old, missing for three days, found listening and asking questions among the teachers.
screen: `THE BOY IN THE TEMPLE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: questions belong in the temple. Today, ask one real question you've been holding, out loud, to someone you trust. Day forty-six.

howItsDone: Many churches read this story in the Christmas season, and Catholics pray it as the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary, the finding in the temple. Bible study groups and confirmation classes often begin from it, since it shows the young Jesus asking questions.

fork.setup: you're Mary. after three days you find your son among the teachers in the temple. what do you say?
options: nothing. just hug him and leave.
son, why have you done this to us? we searched for you, sorrowing.
scold him in front of everyone.
fork.reveal: Mary asks why, and says his father and she sought him sorrowing. his answer, about his Father's business, is the first thing Jesus says in Luke.

original.note: Greek: teacher. Luke finds the boy in the midst of the teachers; later, people will call him teacher too.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a clever child showing off.
what it means: a boy listening and asking questions in the house of God, and parents who don't yet understand.
what a scholar hears: his first words in Luke, en tois tou patros mou, can mean my Father's business or my Father's house, and translators still choose between them.

notes: 'The first thing Jesus says in Luke's Gospel' — Luke 2:49 is his first recorded speech in Luke; confirm.
Luke 2:49 Greek ἐν τοῖς τοῦ πατρός μου is ambiguous ('my Father's house' or 'my Father's affairs'); KJV has 'business'.

'The only story in the four Gospels from the years between infancy and adult life' refers to the canonical Gospels (later non-canonical infancy gospels exist). 'Eighteen years or so' assumes Luke 3:23 ('about thirty years of age'); confirm.
The script avoids calling this a bar mitzvah (a later custom, at thirteen).
Finding in the Temple is the fifth joyful mystery of the rosary; confirm.
